blocks.text: Apoptosis occurs in two steps: Initiation and execution. The initiation phase contains extrinsic and intrinsic pathways.
The extrinsic pathway of apoptosis starts outside the cells in the following order:

items.text: Presence of Fas/CD95 on the outer part of the cell membrane
Binding of Fas/CD95 ligand of T cells to Fas
Trimerization of Fas
Formation of FADD (Fas-associated death domain)
Activation of caspase 8, 10 (by conversion of procaspase 8 and 10 to caspase 8 and 10)

blocks.text: In intrinsic pathway, caspase 9 is activated.

The Apoptosome is a multi-protein complex that plays a critical role in the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis, formed when cytochrome C (Cyt C) is released from mitochondria into the cytosol in response to cellular stress or damage.
Once in the cytosol:

items.text: Cytochrome c binds to Apaf-1 (apoptotic protease activating factor-1) in the presence of dATP/ATP
This triggers the formation of the apoptosome complex
The apoptosome then recruits and activates procaspase-9, which leads to activation of downstream executioner caspases (3, 6, 7)

blocks.text: Structurally, apoptosomes are comprising of wheel-like hexamer configuration.

Fas ligand is a component of Apoptosis and not efferocytosis. Efferocytosis: The apoptotic bodies give the eat-me signals, which are expressed as C1q, Thrombospondin, and PS (Phosphatidyl Serine). In the normal cell, the Phosphatidyl Serine is present in the inner leaflet, but in the apoptotic cell, it comes out. This is known as Phosphatidyl Serine Flipping (Defective in Scott syndrome).

Based on this flipping, the Macrophage engulfs the apoptotic bodies, which is called Efferocytosis. Fas ligand is not an eat-me signal; it is a component of the initiating pathway via which apoptosis starts.
Defect of flipping of Phosphatidyl Serine: Scott syndrome: Affects apoptosis and platelet function.
Note: Cancer cells express CD47 to Macrophages. CD47 is a "Do not Eat me" signal.

Pattern B shows discrete DNA bands at regular intervals. This is characteristic of internucleosomal cleavage into fragments of ~180–200 base pairs. Such a “DNA ladder” is a hallmark of apoptotic cell death.
DNA Fragmentation Patterns in Cell Death (Agarose Gel Electrophoresis)

items.text: **Apoptosis:** Mechanism: Specific endonucleases cleave DNA at internucleosomal regions. Gel Pattern: Produces a "DNA ladder" with regular 180–200 bp fragments. Diagnostic Value: Presence of ladder indicates programmed cell death.

**Necrosis:** Mechanism: Random, widespread DNA degradation due to cellular disintegration. Gel Pattern: Appears as a diffuse smear without defined bands. Diagnostic Value: Smear indicates uncontrolled or accidental cell death.

blocks.title: Apoptosis vs Necrosis on Agarose Gel

blocks.text: Caspase 1 and the inflammasome are the entities responsible for a form of cell death known as Pyroptosis. A form of apoptosis in which there is release of the fever-inducing cytokine IL-1. Seen in response to bacterial infections like Salmonella and Shigella. Microbial products entering infected cells are recognized by cytoplasmic receptors, activating the multiprotein complex inflammasome. Inflammasome activates caspases 1, 4, 5, and 11. They will together result in the killing of the cell (apoptosis). Caspase 1, which converts the inactive IL-1 to active IL-1, causing fever, inflammation and leucocyte recruitment

blocks.text: Necroptosis is a caspase-independent programmed cell death. Programmed necrosis is also known as Necroptosis.

blocks.text: Anoikis is a type of cell death which prevents metastasis. A type of apoptosis in which the cell undergoes programmed cell death when cells detach from the surrounding extracellular matrix (ECM) or neighbouring cells. When cancer cells detach from the primary tumor, they are susceptible to anoikis.
Acts as a barrier against the survival and dissemination of these detached cancer cells
Anoikis is a type of cell death which, if occurs, prevents spread of cancer or metastasis.
Telomerase prevents the shortening of telomeres by adding DNA sequences to the ends of chromosomes, thus potentially extending cells' lifespan.
**Telomere:** It is the sequence present on the terminal of chromosomes. Ageing is due to the shortening of telomeres as the person grows.
Telomerase, also known as the immortality gene, is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase enzyme that adds DNA sequences to the ends of chromosomes, preventing telomere shortening during cell division.
Sirtuins are a family of NAD-dependent protein deacetylases produced by SIRT genes (SIRT1-7) that play a key role in DNA repair mechanisms and are involved in maintaining genomic stability
Functions/benefits of sirtuins:

items.text: Anti-ageing
Prevents telomerase from shortening (Option A ruled out)
Cell repair
Increases the insulin sensitivity of tissues: Beneficial for DM patients and slows down ageing. (Option D ruled out)
Sirtuins are histone deacetylases (Option C ruled out)
Sirtuins increase insulin sensitivity

blocks.text: The clinical presentation points towards Werner syndrome, also known as Adult Progeria Syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by premature ageing features that typically manifest in adulthood. It is associated with a DNA helicase defect.

items.text: **Hutchinson-Gilford Syndrome (Option A):** It is a rare genetic progeroid syndrome characterized by severe premature ageing features that begin in childhood. It is a Laminopathy due to a Lamin-A (LMNA) gene mutation.
**Wermer Syndrome (Option C):** Wermer Syndrome is for as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1).
**Cockayne Syndrome (Option D):** It is also a rare autosomal recessive progeroid syndrome. However, it typically presents in childhood. ERCC gene defect.

blocks.text: Autophagy (aka cell cannibalism) is a cellular process by which a cell eats its own contents and plays a critical role in maintaining cellular homeostasis, responding to stressors such as nutrient deprivation, and eliminating potentially harmful cellular materials.
Autophagy has 4 types:

items.text: **Macro-autophagy:** Eats substrate by forming a membrane around it (Autophagosome)
**Micro-autophagy:** Eats substrate by endocytosis
Chaperone-mediated autophagy
**Mitophagy:** Mitochondria are eaten
**Marker of autophagy:** LC3
**Most important gene for autophagy:** ATG1 gene

blocks.text: In chaperone-mediated autophagy, chaperone proteins (Eg, Heat shock proteins) recognize and bind to specific protein substrates that are misfolded or damaged. The chaperone-substrate complex then interacts with the lysosomal-associated membrane protein LAMP2A, facilitating the substrate protein's translocation into the lysosome for degradation.

items.text: **Direct uptake by lysosomes via endocytosis (Option A):** is mechanism is observed in Microautophagy.
**Inhibition of mTOR leading to activation of ULK1 complex (Option B):** is seen in Macroautophagy.
**Selective degradation of damaged or dysfunctional mitochondria (Option C):** is seen in Mitophagy.

blocks.text: LC3, or Microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3, is a reliable marker of autophagy.
**Most important gene for autophagy:** ATG1 gene

items.text: **Annexin A1 (Option A):** Annexin A1 is a marker of hairy cell leukaemia.
**Annexin 5 (Option B):** Marker of apoptosis
**Beclin 1 (Option C):** Beclin-1 is not a direct marker of autophagy but plays a crucial role in initiating autophagy

blocks.text: Hypertrophy results from increased cellular protein production, while hyperplasia involves growth factor-driven proliferation of mature cells.

rows: Hypertrophy is characterized by increased cellular protein (GATA4, NFAT, MEF2) production, which leads to the enlargement of cells and tissues due to an increase in cell size. An increase in cellular proteins occurs either through enhanced central dogma processes (transcription and translation) or through an increase of transcription factors.
Hyperplasia is described as the result of growth factor-driven proliferation of mature cells. In hyperplasia, the number of cells within an organ or tissue increases.

items.text: Hypertrophy involves an increase in cell size, while hyperplasia involves an increase in cell number. (Option A ruled out)
Both hypertrophy and hyperplasia increase tissue mass. (Option B ruled out)
Hypertrophy can be reversible. (Option C ruled out)

rows: Increase in the size of cells or organs.

Cell enlargement occurs in response to increased workload or stress

An increase in the number of cells in response to hormonal or growth factor stimulation.
Breast glandular epithelium proliferation during puberty or pregnancy.
Occurs when there is an abnormal increase in the number of cells in an organ or tissue due to excessive or inappropriate hormonal or growth factor stimulation

blocks.text: Reduction in thymus gland size during ageing is an example of physiological atrophy.

Physiological atrophy refers to the normal, programmed decrease in the size or mass of tissues, organs, or structures in the body. The thymus gland, which is involved in the development of the immune system, tends to decrease in size and activity with age, which is an example of physiological atrophy.
Pathological atrophy, on the other hand, refers to the abnormal decrease in the size or mass of tissues, organs, or structures due to disease, injury, or other abnormal conditions.
Testicular atrophy, intestinal atrophy and brain atrophy are examples of pathological atrophy. (Options A, B, D ruled out)

Disuse atrophy is seen in a patient with smaller, weaker muscles after being bedridden for several weeks. During prolonged periods of immobility, such as extended bed rest, the muscles experience decreased mechanical loading and activity. This lack of stimulation decreases muscle protein synthesis and increases protein breakdown, resulting in muscle wasting and weakness.

items.text: **Neurogenic atrophy (Option B):** Atrophy due to hampered nerve supply. E.g.- In polio patients, the muscle will become immobile, leading to neurogenic atrophy.
**Endocrine atrophy (Option C):** Atrophy due to a decrease in hormones. E.g. - A decrease in the level of estrogens leading to endometrial atrophy, which is seen in postmenopausal women.
**Senile atrophy (Option D):** Seen in old age and in patients with Alzheimer's disease.

blocks.text: Barrett's oesophagus is characterized by the replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus with columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. (Goblet cells contain acidic mucin staining positive with alcian blue, which helps to differentiate from intestinal epithelium)
This metaplastic change is considered an adaptive response to chronic exposure to gastric acid and bile reflux in the setting of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
